props.title: The Walker

sections.content: Paul Schrader's **The Walker** (2007) follows in the sophisticated footsteps of his earlier character study **American Gigolo** (1980), examining the life of a professional "walker" - wealthy women's platonic escort - in Washington D.C.'s political circles. Woody Harrelson delivers a nuanced performance as Carter Page III, a gay socialite whose carefully constructed world unravels when he becomes entangled in a murder investigation. The film connects thematically to other political thrillers like **The Good Shepherd** (2006) and **Michael Clayton** (2007), exploring the dark underbelly of power structures while maintaining a measured, almost European pace.

sections.content: **The Walker** (2007) sits within a rich tradition of films examining social gatekeepers and power brokers, from **La Dolce Vita** (1960) to **Dangerous Liaisons** (1988). Schrader's direction emphasizes the suffocating formality of Washington society, using precise framing and muted colors to create an atmosphere of privileged containment. The film's exploration of gay identity in conservative political circles predates later works like **Milk** (2008) and **J. Edgar** (2011), offering a subtle commentary on sexuality and power.

Like Schrader's other character studies - **Light Sleeper** (1992), **Affliction** (1997) - The Walker delves into moral corruption and personal isolation. Harrelson's Carter Page III joins Travis Bickle (**Taxi Driver**, 1976) and Julian Kay (**American Gigolo**, 1980) in Schrader's gallery of lonely men navigating hostile environments. The film's murder mystery elements serve as a framework for deeper examination of loyalty, privilege, and the price of belonging. SUBHEAD: Political Power and Social Commentary

sections.content: The film's Washington D.C. setting places it within a lineage of political thrillers like **All the President's Men** (1976) and **Primary Colors** (1998), but Schrader subverts expectations by focusing on the social rather than institutional aspects of power. This approach aligns with films like **The Devil Wears Prada** (2006) and **Marie Antoinette** (2006), which examine how social hierarchies maintain and perpetuate power structures.
